posts.text:
BREAKING: This past week's -10.4% drop in the Nasdaq 100 was one of the rarest weekly declines in 40 years.

Of the last 2,133 trading weeks, just 11 saw declines of this magnitude or worse.

That's 0.52% of all weeks, a 3.27 standard deviation move based on the historical mean and volatility.

Of course, market returns exhibit "fat tails," meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.

However, even accounting for the fact that extreme market moves are more common than traditional statistical models suggest, this was a historically rare selloff.

Volatility returns when markets least expect it.

US stocks have rarely been this oversold:

The S&P 500 closed the week 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, its widest deviation since August 2015.

This also marks its 3rd-largest deviation in at least 20 years.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, the index’s largest deviation from its 50-DMA was 3.6 standard deviations.

Not even the 2020 Pandemic crash saw such extreme oversold conditions, with the S&P 500 falling 3.8 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average in February.

During the 2022 bear market and the April 2025 post-"Liberation Day" selloff, the S&P 500 fell 3.2 and 3.3 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, respectively.

This has been one of the sharpest market sell-offs in history.

Prices of imported computers and semiconductors are skyrocketing:

US import prices for computers, peripherals, and semiconductors surged +26.5% YoY in October, their largest annual increase on record in data going back to the 1990s.

This also marks the 7th consecutive YoY increase of at least +10.0%.

MoM, the US Import Price Index for computers, peripherals, and semiconductors rose +3.6%, to 61.1 points, its highest level since December 2008.

Since March 2025, this figure has soared +30.0%, reversing its long-term downwtrend.

The AI investment boom is reversing decades of falling electronics prices.

BREAKING: AI-related investment contributed +1.27 percentage points to real US GDP growth in Q1 through Q3 2026.

This represents ~65% of the economy's cumulative growth of ~2% over this period.

Software investment contributed the most, at +0.45 percentage points, followed by computers and peripheral equipment, at +0.37 percentage points.

Communication and electrical equipment contributed +0.21 percentage points, R&D +0.16 percentage points, and data center structures +0.07 percentage points.

AI investment has become the backbone of the US economy.

Market sentiment has taken a complete 180 degree turn:

The Fear & Greed Index fell to 9.7 points on Friday, below 10.0 for the first time since March 2026.

This marks its 4th lowest level since the 2022 bear market.

A reading below 30.0 indicates "Extreme Fear" territory and oversold market conditions.

The index has fallen -30.6 points, or -76%, over the last 6 trading sessions, its sharpest decline since February 2025.

The last 3 times the Fear & Greed Index fell below 10.0, the S&P 500 rallied +10.5% on average over the next 3 weeks.

Since 2021, the S&P 500 has gained +9.0% on average over the 3 weeks following readings below 10.0.

Sentiment is extremely polarized right now.

Anthropic is sitting on an enormous cash pile:

Anthropic's cash and cash equivalents are up to a record $237 billion following its IPO.

This comes as its IPO raised $81 billion, with another $26 billion secured through a private placement with selected investors.

By comparison, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, SpaceX, $SPCX, and Apple, $AAPL, each hold less than 25% of this amount.

Anthropic's cash pile is therefore larger than those 4 companies combined.

This is also 8 times Nvidia's, $NVDA, cash balance, 12 times Microsoft's, $MSFT, and 22 times Meta's, $META.

For perspective, Berkshire Hathaway’s cash pile stands at $377 billion.

Anthropic has a huge amount of cash to deploy.

BREAKING: Gold is now on track for its worst 3-month rolling performance since June 2013, down -21.6% since the start of September.

This would also mark gold's largest 3-month rolling price decline since 1981.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, gold's biggest 3-month drawdown was -22.2%.

Meanwhile, silver prices are down -38.7% since the start of September, putting them on track for their biggest 3-month rolling decline since 2008, when prices fell -45.3%.

By comparison, silver's largest 3-month rolling decline on record was -63.6% in 1980.

Gold and silver are experiencing historic selling pressure.
